title: Wave motion and energy transfer

learning_outcomes.text: describe what is meant by wave motion as illustrated by vibration in ropes, springs and ripple tanks
understand that energy is transferred by a progressive wave

prior_knowledge_summary: AS Topic 1 quantities, units, scalars and vectors.
new_learning: Particles of a medium oscillate locally while the disturbance travels.
A progressive wave transfers energy without a net transfer of the medium.
not_yet_taught: amplitude, period, frequency, wavelength and phase as measured quantities

blocks.heading: A pulse arrives, but what travelled?
content: Imagine a long rope with a strip of tape tied near its middle. You flick one end once. A pulse moves along the rope and reaches the far end, yet the tape only moves away from its resting position and comes back.
Predict what you would see if the rope material itself travelled with the pulse. Would the tape finish near the far end?

figure.purpose: Separate the travelling pulse from the local motion of one marked rope element.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch in two time frames. Show a rope pulse farther right in the second frame while the same taped point moves up then returns. Use sparse arrows and two colours for pulse travel and tape motion.
figure.alt_text: Two snapshots show a pulse moving right along a rope while one taped point moves locally and does not travel with the pulse.

blocks.heading: A travelling disturbance
content: The flick disturbs the first small section of rope. That section pulls on the next section, which then pulls on the next. The pattern travels because neighbouring sections interact.
Each section moves for a short time around its own equilibrium position. It does not follow the pulse along the whole rope. The travelling pattern and the moving material are different things.

figure.purpose: Show the causal neighbour-to-neighbour transfer that makes a disturbance travel.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper three-step sequence of a segmented rope. Highlight successive neighbouring sections as the pulse passes. Include a rightward pattern arrow and short local motion arrows.
figure.alt_text: A three-step rope sequence shows neighbouring sections moving in turn as the disturbance travels right.

blocks.heading: The same idea in a spring and a ripple tank
content: Push and release one end of a stretched spring. A crowded region can move along the spring while each coil shifts briefly and returns. Drop a small cork on water as ripples pass. The ripple spreads outward while the cork mainly bobs near one place.
Rope, spring and water look different, but the causal story is the same. One region is disturbed, it affects a neighbouring region, and a travelling disturbance results.

figure.purpose: Compare travelling disturbance with local medium motion in the three syllabus examples.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison table with small hand sketches of rope, spring and ripple tank. Use one column for travelling disturbance and one for local element motion. Keep labels conceptual and avoid later wave-type terms.
figure.alt_text: Rope, spring and ripple tank sketches compare the travelling disturbance with local motion of rope sections, coils and a cork.

blocks.heading: Progressive waves carry energy
content: A pulse can make the far end of a rope move, a water ripple can rock a floating cork, and a sound wave can make an eardrum vibrate. Something reaches the new place and can cause a change. That transferred quantity is energy.
Definition to learn: a progressive wave is a wave that transfers energy from place to place.
The wave carries energy through the chain of interactions. The medium supplies the particles that interact, but the medium does not need to travel with the energy.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: a wave that transfers energy from place to place

figure.purpose: Link an input action to a distant observable effect through energy transfer.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper energy pathway sketch: hand flicks rope at left, pulse travels, lightweight marker at right moves. Use a coloured energy arrow along the rope and local motion arrows at the marker.
figure.alt_text: A hand sends a pulse along a rope and a distant marker moves, showing energy transferred from place to place.

blocks.heading: Why it can look as if matter travels
content: It is reasonable to think that the rope or water travels with the visible shape. Our eyes naturally follow the moving crest or pulse as one object.

That model fails when we track one marked piece of the medium. The mark moves locally and returns near equilibrium while the disturbance continues onward. A stadium wave gives another picture: the raised pattern circles the stadium, but each person only stands and sits near one seat.
Correct the model by tracking two things separately: the travelling disturbance and one material element.

figure.purpose: Repair the common belief that the medium moves forward with the wave.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper before-and-after concept sketch. Left shows the tempting but crossed-out idea of a marked rope section riding with the pulse. Right shows the pulse advancing while the mark returns near its original horizontal position.
figure.alt_text: A crossed-out model shows matter riding with a pulse, beside the correct model where the pulse advances and the marked material stays local.

blocks.heading: Follow one cork, then follow the ripple
content: A cork floats near the centre of a ripple tank. A straight ripple passes it and later reaches a small floating gate farther away.
First follow the cork. It moves around its equilibrium position as the ripple passes, then remains near the same part of the tank. This describes the local motion of the medium.
Now follow the ripple. The disturbance travels from the source, past the cork and to the gate. When the gate moves, it confirms that energy reached a new place.
Independent check: if the water had travelled from the source to the gate with the ripple, the cork would have been carried across the tank. It was not.

figure.purpose: Model a two-track reasoning procedure that follows the medium and disturbance separately.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper top-view ripple tank sequence with source, cork and gate. Show ripple fronts at three times, a short cork-motion arrow and a long disturbance/energy route to the gate.
figure.alt_text: Three ripple-tank moments show a ripple travelling from source past a cork to a gate while the cork remains near one place.

blocks.heading: The two-track wave model
content: For any wave-motion example, ask two questions. What pattern or disturbance travels? What does one particle or marked part of the medium do?
A progressive wave transfers energy from place to place. The particles of the medium oscillate locally about equilibrium, passing the disturbance onward through interactions.
Do not yet use the shape of a diagram to name a wave type. In later lessons, direction, measured wave quantities and graph meanings will be added to this model.

figure.purpose: Summarise the distinction learners should apply in practice.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper concept map with two branches from wave motion: travelling disturbance transfers energy; medium element oscillates locally. Add small rope, spring and ripple icons as examples.
figure.alt_text: A concept map separates the travelling energy-carrying disturbance from the local oscillation of the medium.

visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

concepts_taught: energy transfer without net transport of the medium
misconceptions_addressed: The material of the medium travels with the visible wave shape.
next_lesson_can_assume: A progressive wave transfers energy from place to place.
The disturbance travels while a medium element oscillates locally about equilibrium.
Wave motion can be illustrated with ropes, springs and ripple tanks.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Definitions or measurements of amplitude, period, frequency or wavelength.
